Well, good afternoon everyone. Thank you so much for being here today. We're very pleased to be joined by Julien Harnais, the Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Yemen. And Julien, without further ado, I give you the floor. I think everybody knows what you will be talking about today.

Okay, good afternoon. Thank you for making the time. My name is Julian Hannes. I'm the UN Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator for Yemen, and I'm today speaking to you from Sana'a. I wanted to talk about generally the humanitarian situation in Yemen and the consequences of the recent airstrikes yesterday in Aden, as well as in the airport where I was present. So in Yemen, we have, as a result of the 10-year conflict, 18 million people in need of humanitarian assistance. That's about half the population. Next year, as a result of worsening economic conditions, Not so much active fighting, but because of the worsening economy. We expect that number to increase to 19 million. That means that Yemen, in absolute terms, is the second-highest case number— caseload of children, malnourished children. It also means that Yemen is the second-highest caseload of people who are not able to reach health services. This is absolute numbers, not percentages. Which is the 3rd highest number of food insecure people in the world. So we are looking at a massive humanitarian situation. We expect that number to increase to 19 million next year, 2025. This could get much worse because that is based upon scenarios and our understanding of the situation as it was a couple of months ago. As we look at the possibility of further violence between Ansar Allah in the north of the country and Israel, there could be further impact on civilian infrastructure, harbor, airports, and roads, which would lead to immense suffering of the Yemeni population. The airstrikes on the harbor are particularly concerning. Yemen imports approximately 80% of its foodstuffs So, if Hodeidah harbor is disabled, that means that the whole of the population of northern Yemen, which is about 65 to 70% of the population, will be in increased humanitarian need. Yesterday, I was at the airport when the airstrikes hit— well, destroyed the air traffic control killed the staff who were working there and injured my UNHCR crew member colleague who was there with the flight. And the airstrikes landed approximately 300 meters away from where Director-General Tedros was and myself. There was one airstrike approximately 300 meters to the south of us and about another airstrike about 300 meters to the north of us. What was most frightening about that airstrike wasn't the effect on us, is that the airstrikes took place as a civilian airliner from Yemen carrying hundreds of Yemenis was about to land. And in fact, the— that airliner from Yemen was landing, taxiing in when the air traffic control was destroyed. Fortunately, that plane was able to land safely and the passengers were able to disembark, but it could have been far, far worse. And so the airport of Sinai is a civilian infrastructure. It is the location whereby all of the international humanitarian aid workers who work in the north of the country come in and leave by. So if that airport is disabled, it will paralyze the humanitarian operations. It's also the airport by which thousands of Yemenis who are unable to get decent healthcare, advanced healthcare in the country, leave to go either to Jordan or to Cairo, eventually to Mumbai, to get advanced healthcare. So it is an absolutely vital humanitarian location. It is essential that all parties to the conflict observe scrupulously international humanitarian law throughout these exchanges. So that's the kind of very quick overview, and I'm very happy to take any questions that you might have. Thank you.

Okay, thank you, Edith. So we were a party of approximately 20 UN personnel in, in 5 vehicles. I'm based in Yemen and had previously received Director-General Tedros some 2 days before. He'd previously been in Aden and had traveled up to Sana'a. And we have been engaged in a long-running negotiation in order to obtain the release of our colleagues. And Director-General Tedros had visited Aden to meet with the government of Yemen there, and then had traveled up to Sana'a to discuss with the authorities how to obtain the release of our colleagues. And I was with the Director-General throughout those discussions. We were in the— in a VIP room, which is next to the main terminal. As you can imagine, Sana'a Airport is a— Sana'a International Airport is a very— is a relatively small building compared to most international airports. And the airstrikes were approximately 16:43, so at about quarter to 5 p.m. Okay. And not only obviously did we have zero indication of any potential airstrikes, but we cannot remember the last time there were airstrikes in Sana'a during daylight hours. And the Saudi coalition has paused their military operations some 2 years ago. But during the period they're operating, they would tend to bomb at night. The US and UK coalition, which has been retaliating or responding to Ansar Allah strikes and missiles in the Red Sea, have tended to bomb at after mid— after 11 p.m. at night to early mornings. So An airstrike on a civilian location in the middle of the day, just before an Airbus A320 was about to land, and as a UN party was there, was completely unexpected.

Just a quick follow-up, which I'm sure we all want to know. So what happened when, when the airstrike took place? What, what did you all do? Did people fall, go to fall on the, you know, go to the ground, go under furniture?

They moved the colleagues out of the VIP building into 5 armored vehicles that were waiting for the delegation. And we, we waited in the armored vehicles for approximately 40 minutes so that we could ascertain what has been— what was the situation, and so that we could also look after the injured crew member. One of the UNHAS crew members was hit in the lower leg with an open— by shrapnel, who lost a lot of blood. I saw the blood on the tarmac this morning as we said goodbye to Tedros. He lost a lot of blood and had to be evacuated to a hospital inside Sana'a. So We stayed to make sure that the crew were okay and evacuate them to the center of Sana'a and to make sure it was safe for us to move. And thank you for the questions, Edith.

And, um, uh, in order— before we could fly, obviously we needed to check the damage to the runway. And to be— and also to see how the operation on the UNHAS crew member went. He went for 4 hours of surgery, and fortunately we've been able to move him out with Director General Cedros. this afternoon.

Okay. Thank you so much for the question. So on the detention, As I noted before, some 100 persons were detained in June of this year, and of which 13 of them are UN personnel. And then a further 4 UN personnel were detained in 2021 and 2023. In total, 17 persons have been detained, approximately 6 weeks ago, one person, one UN personnel was released and 2 NGO persons were also released. The— all of our persons, all of the UN colleagues who have been detained have been working on humanitarian and aid projects throughout this period, and they are covered by UN privileges and immunities, and they should not be detained. And we have repeatedly called upon the authorities in Sana'a for their release. We have seen over the last weeks some slight improvements, but one person have been able to speak with their families at least one occasion. And as I noted, one UN personnel and 2 NGOs were released some 6 weeks ago. The discussions that myself and Director-General Tedros engaged in here were to seek a way forward so that all UN personnel and non-UN personnel, NGOs and civil society, could be released. In our discussions with various senior officials in Sana'a, they gave us commitments That we hope will lead to the eventual release of our colleagues. And in terms of the— I'll sort of stop there and then I'll move on to the discussion about the harbor.

So the—

as we noted, 80% of UN's food comes through Hodeidah Harbor for the— sorry, 80% of Yemen's food requirements for the north comes through Hodeida Harbor. And I would say close to 90%, 95% of the medical supplies. So the harbor is absolutely vital. If that harbor is decapacitated, and there have been numerous airstrikes on that harbor, there was airstrikes twice yesterday, Some days ago, the tugs which are used to bring in the big ships, 2 tugs were destroyed. And there have been previous airstrikes in and around the harbor over the last months. And the— if that harbor does not operate, then we will see a dramatic and sudden decrease in the humanitarian situation in Yemen. The harbor is a civilian location, and the Security Council has established 2 missions to— in order to assure that. One is the UNMAHA, which was set up as a result of the Stockholm Agreement, and their purpose is to ensure that the harbor is used only for civilian purposes. The other UN mission is UNVIM, So the United Nations Verification Inspection Mechanism, which is not based in Yemen but is actually based in Djibouti. They are responsible for ensuring that all containers and products that are taken into Hodeida harbor are consistent with Security Council resolutions. So there's 2 UN missions whose only job is to ensure that Hodeida remains only of use for civilian Civilian reasons. So it's a civilian facility, there is no doubt about that. And, and with the UN works to ensure that, and any damage to it will lead to massive suffering for Yemenis. Thank you.

So we're still—

It is not— we have a protocol for all humanitarian workers to inform various parties to the conflict. I won't go into the details precisely which parties to the conflict we inform, but I think the bigger issue is parties to the conflict have an obligation to ensure that they are not striking a civilian target and not striking civilians. The obligation is on them, not on us. We don't need to prove we're civilians. They need to prove that they are hitting a military target. Sana'a Airport has not been a military target since 2016. I was, I was in Yemen at the beginning of the conflict, and I remember the day when all of the military capacities were destroyed at Sana'a Airport. And that was, that was 4 years, 9 years ago. And Sana'a Airport has subsequently been repeatedly bombed over the, you know, for many years. So it's a civilian location. It is used by the United Nations. It's used by the International Committee for the Red Cross. It is used for civilian flights. That is its purpose. And so all parties to the conflict have an obligation to respect the civilian nature of that facility and to observe international humanitarian law. The responsibility is on them. Thank you.

Thank you, Adrien. That's a very humane question. The, um, you know, the, the conditions both as a result— I mean, obviously, firstly, there's a result of the detention, um, not just UN personnel but also NGO personnel, and we're completely perturbed. Um, I had many colleagues who for weeks were very anxious about even coming to the office or going out on field missions. And similarly for NGO staff, and, you know, even for myself, you know, I sort of, you know, I was thinking about, goodness, what if they, you know, sort of start trawling— somebody picks up my phone and starts trawling through all my WhatsApp messages with my wife or something, you know. And, you know, when you're in that kind of environment, you're operating in that environment, it's very heavy for everyone. And then in addition, so you've got those challenges, and we've seen some improvements in the operating conditions in the last, say, 2, 3 months. And there's been some changes in the personnel in the authorities in Sana'a, which has meant that some of the problems that we saw have reduced. So we have been having— international staff have no longer been asked to leave Yemen, which was the case up until about 3, 4 months ago, where every week we would have an international staff member asked to leave. And the discussions that we have with the authorities now are much more focused and directed towards finding solutions for Yemenis in need, The agreements which were so difficult to achieve in the past have— for both the UN and NGOs, we've been able to rapidly conclude those. So we've seen some improvements in the operating conditions, and that has reduced the, to a certain extent, the concerns among Yemeni staff. But obviously, when they still see that 16 of their colleagues are detained and INGO staff and national NGO staff are detained, there's obviously a great deal of anxiety. Then if you add in, in addition to that, airstrikes and the fear of more airstrikes, the concerns, the fear of, you know, what's going to happen next. Are we going to see attacks against bridges, roads, electricity systems and other civilian infrastructure? What does that mean for them? As you know, we have 3,000 staff across the country and we're moving around constantly. And, you know, what's going to happen to them? And obviously, you know, we follow the news and we see what happens in other countries. And, you know, my staff and not just my staff, NGO staff and, you know, health workers in government clinics, they look at that and there's a lot of fear. So, you know, it's very difficult to keep people focused and working for vulnerable Yemenis. But fortunately, that is the case. They, you know, everybody's getting on with what's required. But it is a very challenging environment.

in terms— so we met, Director-General Tedros and myself met the— and I'll be using titles which they use to refer to themselves, right? The Prime Minister of the Government of Change and Reconstruction.
